newsitem.title: BELGIUM: No such thing as a quiet time in competition field.
newsitem.headline: No such thing as a quiet time in competition field.

text.p: With the row over the Volkswagen subsidies temporarily defused, the autumn looks clear of high-profile, politically sensitive, competition cases.

But there is no such thing as a slack period in the competition field and there is every sign that the European Commission will re-open the file on Credit Lyonnais -- once Europe's largest bank -- which only a year ago benefited from one of the biggest rescue plans in European banking history.
The following are the merger, state aid and other cases on which there may be a decision or key development before the end of 1996.
MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS
Thanks to the strict deadlines set in the merger regulation 4064/89 this is the most predictable competition area.
Four cases are currently being examined under the second phase investigation, which is more than usual. This reflects a new restructuring wave in European industry.
The opening of a second phase, which takes a total of four months, usually means the deal concerned will have to be changed to meet the demands of EU competition rules.

- Cablevision, the Spanish cable joint venture between the Spanish subsidiary of Canal Plus, Spain's telecommunications giant Telefonica and Sociedad de Gestion de Cable SA, is the first on the list. Deadline is the second half of November.

After fighting hard to get the deal submitted to its jurisdiction -- something the companies involved are still questioning in the European Court -- the Commission expressed "serious doubts" that it would close the Spanish markets for cable and pay-television as well as phone and data transmission services.
The case, like the Unisource telecoms deal, provides the Commission with a golden oportunity to break open earlier than expected the monopoly operated by state-controlled Telefonica.

- The Commission is also due to rule by the end of November on the Finnish supermarket deal involving Kesko Oy and Tuko Oy. The merger does not have an EU dimension, but Finland submitted it to the Commission because it has no legislation to deal with creation of dominant positions.
In opening its detailed investigation the Commission said the deal "could lead to high market shares" in Finland with respect to daily consumer products.

- The Commission also started a full probe into a deal that would unite the two largest producers of silicon carbide in western Europe under the leadership of France's giant group Saint-Gobain. Silicon carbide is a mineral used mainly in the making of abrasives and heat-resistant products. Deadline is early December.

- Finally, it announced last week it had started a full probe into the acquisition by Coca-Cola Enterprises Inc of Amalgamated Beverages Great Britain Ltd, which owns the British bottler for Coca-Cola and Cadbury Schweppes brands of soft drinks.

The most important cases currently going through the routine one-month inquiry stage include the merger of the television units of German media giant Bertelsmann and its Luxembourg-based counterpart CLT. The Commission has been acting particularly tough in the media sector.
STATE AID

- The Commission is currently probing compliance with the July 1995 plan to restructure Credit Lyonnais amid intense speculation that the terms of the plan, which involves maximum subsidies of 45 billion francs, will need to be softened to avoid the bank plunging back into the red.

Commission sources have said there are doubts about whether the plan has been carried out properly, in particular regarding the decision to buy back Societe de Banque Occidentale (SDBO) which had previously been hived off into a special company created to liberate Lyonnais from bad assets. A formal probe is expected to be launched into this issue on Wednesday.

But the bank's more pressing problem, according to the French press, is the huge cost of a loan it granted below market rates to the state-controlled company that took over its bad assets. The loan was one of the prices it had to pay for its reckless expansion in the 80s.
The Commission said last week it had not received any request to change the plan which expires at the end of 1998.

- Two other banks have now followed the Credit Lyonnais to the Commission's door: Italy's largest southern bank Banco di Napoli, and Credit Foncier, another French institution specialised in property lending.

There is a clear feeling at the Commission that the Banco di Napoli case will be much easier to deal with, due partly to the expertise drawn from the Lyonnais case -- which was its first state aid case in the banking sector -- but also because of the apparent Italian desire to cooperate closely with the EU.
Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert himself expressed satisfaction with assurances given by Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi on the case at at meetng in Rome last week.

But he warned that work was only just starting. The Commission started formal proceedings into Italy's plan to inject 2.0 trillion lire into Napoli just before it closed for its summer break and state aid probes usually last many months.

The same applies to the rescue plan for Credit Foncier which involves a credit line of between 20 to 25 billion francs granted by state-controled Caisse des Depots and des Consignations and a 260-billion-franc state guarantee.

In a different area, discussions are likely to speed up between the Commission and Italy on an extension of the period for Italian state industrial holding IRI to reduce its huge debt to levels agreed back in 1992. A compromise emerged during Van Miert's meeting with the Italian government last week that would give IRI until mid 1997 -- the initial deadline was the end of the year -- to cut its debt to 5.0 trillion lire from more than 22 trillion lire in 1995.

In the saga of German aid to its eastern states, which produced damaging confrontations with Bonn during the first half of the year, decisions are awaited in particular on subsidies given to Elf Aquitaine to build a refinery near Leuna, in Sachsen-Anhalt, and unauthorised aid paid to tool maker Gildemeister AG.
Other important state aid cases pending include:
- a Belgian plan to rescue steel maker Clabecq. The Commission is set to start formal proceedings on Wednesday,
- an Austrian proposal to grant 378 million schillings to Hoffmann-Laroche to help it develop Orlistar, a new treatment for obesity,
ARTICLE 85 AND 86
Unlike in the merger area and even more so than in the state aid field, there are no time limits on anti-trust and abuse-of- dominant-position probes.

However, progress was seen in the Unisource deal between telecoms operators Telia AB of Sweden, PTT Telecom BV of Netherlands, Swiss Telecom and Telefonica now that the Atlas/Global One alliances have been cleared.
The Commission has clearly indicated that it will not authorise the joint venture unless Spain agrees to liberalise its market early.

The Commission's approach, similar to that adopted in the Atlas joint venture between France Telecom and Deustche Telekom, is also delaying approval of a subsequent alliance between Unisource and AT&T of the United States called Uniworld.
Under EU rules, telecoms markets must be opened to competition by January 1, 1998 in all but a few countries including Spain, which won a five-year derogation.
The Commission believes that Telefonica, the fifth largest European player, does not really need that extra time.
The Spanish government proposed in July giving up part of the five-year delay. Spanish diplomats expect the negotiations will speed up in the coming months.
Other long-standing cases in the telecoms area concern the America Online computer network and Microsoft Network.

Competition watchers will also be looking for the Commission's verdict on the issue of Dutch soccer television broadcasting rights which was prompted by the launch of the Sport 7 channel and its privileged link with the Dutch football association KNVB.

Similarly, the Commission will have to decide whether to re-draft its decision to exempt the European Broadcasting Union, the Swiss-based association of mainly public TV broadcasters which runs the Eurovision system, from competition rules on the acquisition of sports rights. The European Court annulled the exemption earlier this year.
But Commission sources were not expecting an early decision on any of the high-profile cartel investigations in the insulated pipe, newsprint and plastics industries.
